cards.prompt: A dog-spotting model scores **100%** on a test. But every test photo was one it had trained on, answer included. Does that prove it's good?

options.text: No: it may just remember those photos
Yes: 100% means it got every single photo right
options.nudge: It did, on photos it had already seen with the answers. Would a quiz you'd seen the answers to prove you'd learned?

options.text: Yes, as long as the test used lots of photos
options.nudge: More photos it has already seen still only test its memory. What kind of photo would show what it really learned?

options.text: No: a model can never really score 100% on anything
options.nudge: It can, on photos it has seen before. The real question is which photos it was tested on.

cards.hint: Imagine a school test where you'd seen every question, with the answers, the day before.
cards.explanation: A test it has already seen only checks its **memory**. To find out what a model really learned, you test it on photos it has **never seen**. More of the same photos, or a perfect score on them, proves nothing new.

cards.title: Keep some examples aside
cards.body:
So people split their examples in two. **Training examples** are for learning. **Test examples** are kept aside, and the model never sees them while it learns.

Then you count how many test examples it gets right. **Accuracy** is that as a share: 8 right out of 10 is 80%.

A **fair test** uses new, realistic examples, easy and hard.

cards.prompt: A model is tested on **10** new photos and gets **7** right. What is its accuracy?
cards.hint: With 10 photos, each one is worth 10% of the test.
cards.nudge: Count only the photos it got right. Each of the 10 photos is worth 10%.
cards.explanation: Each photo is worth 10%, and it got 7 right: **70%**. The 3 it got wrong are the other 30%.

cards.prompt:
Memorising isn't learning. A model can learn every detail of its training photos (this dog, this angle, this light) instead of what dogs look like.

A model scores **100%** on its training examples but only **60%** on new test examples. What's the most likely reason?

options.text: Its test examples were much harder than the ones it trained on
options.nudge: Harder tests can lower a score a bit, but a 40-point gap is the classic sign of something else. What does 100% on training suggest?

options.text: It needs more training examples of exactly the same kind
options.nudge: More of the same would make it even better at memorising. What does the gap between the scores tell you?

options.text: It's a good model: 100% on its training data is what counts
options.nudge: Which score shows how it does on examples it has never seen?

options.text: It memorised its training examples instead of the real pattern

cards.hint: Which score shows how it does on examples it has never seen? Why might the two be so different?
cards.explanation: A big gap between training and test scores is the classic sign of **memorising instead of learning**, also called [[overfitting]]. The **test** score (60%) is the one that tells you how it will really do.

cards.prompt: A fair test shows how a model will really do. Is each one a **fair** test, or an **unfair** one?

items.label: Examples kept aside from the start
A mix of easy and hard examples
Changing the test until it scores 100%

cards.hint: A fair test shows how the model will do in real life. Which ones would make it look better than it really is?
cards.nudge: Look for the tests that make the score look good without showing how it does on new, realistic examples.
cards.explanation: Fair tests use **unseen**, **realistic** examples with a **mix** of easy and hard. Testing on its own training examples, only easy ones, or changing the test until it scores 100% all make a model look better than it is.

cards.prompt: A plant model will check photos that gardeners take on their phones, in sun, shade and rain. Which test is the **fairest**?

options.text: 200 new phone photos from different gardens, in all kinds of weather
200 new photos taken by an expert, all in perfect light
options.nudge: They're new, which is good. But are they like the photos it will really meet?

options.text: 200 of its training photos, so the answers are known for sure
options.nudge: Test photos need known answers too. What's wrong with photos it has already learned from?

options.text: 200 new phone photos, picked from ones it already gets right
options.nudge: Picking photos it gets right decides the score before the test starts.

cards.hint: A fair test is new to the model, and like what it will meet for real. Check each option for both.
cards.explanation: Only the **new phone photos in all kinds of weather** are both unseen and realistic. Perfect-light photos make it look better than it will do in a rainy garden, and the other two make the score meaningless.

cards.prompt: A weather model guesses whether it will rain from the clouds and the air. Each training day says what really happened: label them, then see how the model does on **4 test days** it has never seen.

examples.text: Thick cloud, wet air: it rained
examples.label: rain

examples.text: Heavy cloud, damp evening: it rained
examples.label: rain

examples.text: A few clouds, dry air: no rain
examples.label: dry

examples.text: Blue sky, slightly damp air: no rain
examples.label: dry

cards.hint: Each training day ends by saying what really happened. Use that, not your own guess about the weather.
cards.nudge: Read the end of each training day again: it says whether it rained.
cards.explanation: Your labels were right. The model got **3 of the 4** test days right. It called the **cloudy but dry day** rain, because every cloudy day it learned from was also rainy.

cards.prompt: Now add training days so the model gets **all 4** test days right. Three new days are available.

examples.text: Thick cloud, wet air: it rained
examples.label: rain

examples.text: Heavy cloud, damp evening: it rained
examples.label: rain

examples.text: A few clouds, dry air: no rain
examples.label: dry

examples.text: Blue sky, slightly damp air: no rain
examples.label: dry

cards.hint: Which test day did it get wrong? Look for a new training day that's like it.
cards.nudge: Which test day did it get wrong? Find a new training day like it, and check the other test days still pass.
cards.explanation: The model had never seen a **cloudy but dry** day, so it guessed rain. Adding "Overcast, dry evening" fills that gap. Another sunny day doesn't help: the model already knew those. And the cloudy, damp night (no rain) sits right next to a rainy test day, so adding it breaks that one.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Keep **test examples** aside: the model never learns from them.
- **Accuracy** is the share it gets right: 8 of 10 is 80%.
- Perfect on training, poor on new examples? It memorised.

Next: when a model is unfair to some people.
